narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three pieces of information about you drove this outcome, ranked by importance. First, your first-year grades placed you in the bottom decile of your class. Most students who are accepted sit in the middle of their class, around the sixth decile, so your position here strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Second, your LSAT score of 33.5 is noticeably below the average of 37.2 among accepted students; this pulled the prediction back toward success, but not enough to overcome the other factors. Third, your third-year grades again ranked near the bottom of your class (second decile), while accepted students typically sit around the sixth decile. This gave another clear push toward predicting failure.

Taken together, your early and later academic performance in law school sent the strongest signals that you may struggle to pass the bar, outweighing the positive signal from your LSAT.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking tutoring, or enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program before reapplying. Improving your class ranking and practice-test scores will directly address the factors that led to this decision. (218 words)
